subtopic_gates.learner_title: Thermodynamics: State Functions, First Law (Delta U = q + w) & Expansion Work

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: First Law enforces energy conservation: Delta U = q + w; U is a state function (path-independent); q and w are path functions; IUPAC sign convention: heat absorbed by system q > 0, heat released q < 0; work done ON system w > 0 (compression), work done BY system w < 0 (expansion against external pressure: w = -int P_ext dV); In isothermal reversible expansion of ideal gas: w_rev = -2.303 n R T log10(V2/V1).
technical_core.why_required: Thermodynamic energy bookkeeping and pressure-volume mechanical work.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Using engineering sign convention where work done by system is positive.

mandatory_equations.formula: \Delta U = q + w, \quad w_{\text{irrev}} = -P_{\text{ext}} \Delta V, \quad w_{\text{rev}} = -2.303 \, n R T \log_{10}\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)
mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: First Law of Thermodynamics and Reversible/Irreversible PV Work equations
mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: IUPAC sign convention: w = - P_ext Delta V; w < 0 for expansion
mandatory_equations.conditions_of_validity: Ideal gas behavior, closed thermodynamic system

representations.name: Indicator P-V Diagram for Reversible vs Irreversible Gas Expansion
representations.chemistry_encoded: P-V plot comparing smooth hyperbolic curve of reversible isothermal expansion (area = w_rev, maximum magnitude) vs single-step rectangular drop under constant P_ext (area = w_irrev, lower magnitude)
mandatory_labels: Reversible Work Area w_rev = - nRT ln(V2/V1)
Irreversible Single-step Work Area w_irrev = - P_ext (V2 - V1)
State Points: Initial (P1, V1) and Final (P2, V2)
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Negative sign on expansion work under IUPAC convention and larger area for reversible path
representations.common_incorrect_version: Using positive sign for gas expansion work under IUPAC convention
representations.verification_method: Verify Delta U = 0 for isothermal expansion of ideal gas (q = -w)

model_conditions.condition: In free expansion against vacuum (P_ext = 0), work done is identically zero (w = 0).
model_conditions.why_needed: For an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, Delta U = 0 because U depends strictly on temperature; hence q = -w.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Reversible expansion produces the maximum magnitude of work delivered to surroundings.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Identify system, surroundings, and IUPAC signs: heat absorbed q > 0; expansion w < 0.
For isothermal ideal gas, set Delta U = 0 and q = -w.
Evaluate work: w = - P_ext Delta V (irreversible) or w = -2.303 nRT log(V2/V1) (reversible).

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Writing work done by an expanding gas as positive: w = + P Delta V.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Confusing IUPAC chemical convention with traditional mechanical engineering convention.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: Under IUPAC convention, energy leaving the system decreases internal energy; expanding gas does work on surroundings, so w is negative.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: In IUPAC chemical thermodynamics, work is strictly defined as w = - P_ext Delta V, which is negative for expansion.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-THERMO-FIRST-LAW-WORK.

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Entropy (Delta S = q_rev / T), Second Law & Spontaneity of Isolated Systems

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: Entropy S measures statistical molecular disorder / accessible microstates (S = k_B ln W); Delta S = q_rev / T; Second Law of Thermodynamics states that in any spontaneous process, total entropy of the universe increases: Delta S_total = Delta S_system + Delta S_surroundings > 0; For reversible equilibrium, Delta S_total = 0; Entropy increases during melting, boiling, dissolution, and reactions where Delta n_g > 0.
technical_core.why_required: Direction of time arrow and universal thermodynamic irreversibility.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Believing a process cannot be spontaneous if the system's entropy decreases.

mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Second Law total entropy and surroundings entropy relation

symbols.name: Surroundings Entropy Change
symbols.dimension: Entropy transferred to thermal surroundings (-Delta H / T)

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Spontaneity requires Delta S_univ > 0; Delta S_sys can be negative if Delta S_surr is sufficiently positive

representations.name: Microscopic Dispersal of Matter and Energy (Solid -> Liquid -> Gas)
representations.chemistry_encoded: Particulate boxes showing orderly crystalline lattice with low microstates W (solid), fluid mobility with higher W (liquid), and random high-velocity spatial dispersal with maximum W (gas)
mandatory_labels: Low Entropy: Orderly Crystal (Low Microstates W)
High Entropy: Gaseous State (Maximum Positional Dispersal)
Delta S > 0: Sublimation, Vaporization, Delta n_g > 0
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Clear visual representation of increase in positional and energetic disorder
representations.common_incorrect_version: Showing gas with lower entropy than solid
representations.verification_method: Verify S(gas) >> S(liquid) > S(solid) for all substances

model_conditions.condition: Delta S_system alone does NOT govern spontaneity; total entropy Delta S_total = Delta S_sys + Delta S_surr must be positive.
model_conditions.why_needed: Water freezes spontaneously below 0 C even though Delta S_sys < 0 because exothermic freezing releases heat, creating large positive Delta S_surr.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Entropy of pure crystalline substance is zero at absolute zero (Third Law).

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Predict qualitative sign of Delta S_sys: count change in gaseous moles Delta n_g.
Compute Delta S_surr = - Delta H_sys / T.
Evaluate Delta S_total = Delta S_sys + Delta S_surr; spontaneous if > 0.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Believing a reaction cannot be spontaneous if the entropy of the system decreases.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Overlooking the entropy change of the surroundings.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: Water freezing to ice has Delta S_sys < 0, but releases heat into surroundings creating massive Delta S_surr > 0, making Delta S_total > 0.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: Spontaneity requires the TOTAL entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) to increase.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-THERMO-ENTROPY-SECOND-LAW.

problem_families.name: Entropy of Reaction and Total Universe Entropy
problem_families.recognition_cues: Calculate Delta S_sys for 2 H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2 H2O(l) and explain spontaneity at 298 K
problem_families.first_technical_move: Delta S_sys is negative (3 mol gas -> 0 mol gas); highly exothermic reaction makes Delta S_surr = -Delta H/T large positive, so Delta S_univ > 0
problem_families.common_fatal_error: Claiming reaction is non-spontaneous solely because Delta S_sys is negative
problem_families.typical_unknown: Delta S_sys, Delta S_surr, and Delta S_univ

difficulty_profile.difficulty_basis: Statistical thermodynamics, entropy microstates, and second-law irreversibility.

falsification_cases.authoring_defect: Asserting that a spontaneous change can cause the total entropy of an isolated system to decrease.
falsification_cases.expected_failure_reason: In any spontaneous process within an isolated system, entropy must strictly increase (Delta S > 0).

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Gibbs Free Energy (Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S), Spontaneity & Equilibrium

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: Gibbs free energy G = H - TS is the master criterion for spontaneity at constant T and P: Delta G < 0 (spontaneous/exergonic), Delta G = 0 (dynamic equilibrium), Delta G > 0 (non-spontaneous/endergonic); Sign combinations of Delta H and Delta S dictate temperature dependence; Standard free energy links to equilibrium constant: Delta G^\circ = -RT ln K = -2.303 RT log10 K.
technical_core.why_required: Unified criterion combining enthalpy and entropy into single state function.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Believing an endothermic reaction (Delta H > 0) can never be spontaneous at any temperature.

mandatory_equations.formula: \Delta G = \Delta H - T \Delta S, \quad \Delta G^\circ = -R T \ln K = -2.303 \, R T \log_{10} K
mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Gibbs-Helmholtz spontaneity equation and thermodynamic equilibrium relation

symbols.name: Entropy Change
symbols.dimension: Must be converted to kJ/(mol K) by dividing by 1000

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Delta S is typically in J/K while Delta H is in kJ; units must be matched before subtraction

representations.name: Four-Quadrant Gibbs Spontaneity Matrix vs Temperature
representations.chemistry_encoded: 2x2 grid plotting Delta H (+/-) vs Delta S (+/-) showing: Delta H < 0, Delta S > 0 (always spontaneous); Delta H > 0, Delta S < 0 (never spontaneous); Delta H < 0, Delta S < 0 (spontaneous at low T); Delta H > 0, Delta S > 0 (spontaneous at high T where T Delta S dominates)
mandatory_labels: Delta H (-), Delta S (+): Spontaneous at All T (Delta G < 0 always)
Delta H (+), Delta S (-): Non-spontaneous at All T (Delta G > 0 always)
Delta H (-), Delta S (-): Spontaneous at Low T (Enthalpy Driven)
Delta H (+), Delta S (+): Spontaneous at High T (Entropy Driven, T > Delta H/Delta S)
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Clear threshold temperature T_eq = Delta H / Delta S where Delta G = 0
representations.common_incorrect_version: Dividing Celsius temperature in Delta G formula
representations.verification_method: Verify unit consistency (converting Delta S from J to kJ)

model_conditions.condition: Delta S must be converted from J/(mol K) to kJ/(mol K) by dividing by 1000 before evaluating Delta H - T Delta S.
model_conditions.why_needed: Temperature T must strictly be in Kelvin (K = C + 273.15).
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: At equilibrium, Delta G = 0, which yields the transition temperature T_eq = Delta H / Delta S.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Check units: convert Delta S from J/(mol K) to kJ/(mol K).
Apply Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S in Kelvin.
Evaluate sign: Delta G < 0 spontaneous; Delta G = 0 equilibrium; Delta G > 0 non-spontaneous.
Connect to K: compute K = exp(- Delta G^\circ / RT).

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Directly subtracting T Delta S from Delta H without converting Delta S from J to kJ.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Overlooking the 1000-fold metric prefix difference between kJ and J.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: Delta H = -100 kJ and Delta S = -200 J/K at 300 K: subtracting gives -100 - (300)(-200) = +59,900 instead of -100 - (300)(-0.2) = -40 kJ.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: Always divide Delta S by 1000 to convert J to kJ before substituting into Delta G = Delta H - T Delta S.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-THERMO-GIBBS-SPONTANEITY.

problem_families.name: Calculation of Spontaneity Threshold Temperature and K
problem_families.recognition_cues: For reaction with Delta H = +178 kJ/mol and Delta S = +160 J/(mol K), find temperature above which reaction becomes spontaneous
problem_families.first_technical_move: Set Delta G = 0 -> T = Delta H / Delta S = 178 / 0.160 = 1112.5 K (839.3 C)
problem_families.common_fatal_error: Using Delta S = 160 without dividing by 1000, giving absurd temperature 1.1 K
problem_families.typical_unknown: Threshold temperature in K and Celsius

difficulty_profile.difficulty_basis: Free energy optimization, entropy-enthalpy compensation, and equilibrium linkage.

falsification_cases.authoring_defect: Asserting that an endothermic reaction (Delta H > 0) can never be spontaneous under any conditions.
falsification_cases.expected_failure_reason: An endothermic reaction is spontaneous at sufficiently high temperatures if Delta S is positive (T > Delta H / Delta S).

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Dynamic Equilibrium, Equilibrium Constants (Kc, Kp) & Reaction Quotient (Qc)

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic: forward rate = reverse rate; concentrations remain constant; Law of Mass Action gives Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b); Kp = Kc (RT)^Delta n_g; Pure solids and pure liquids have constant active mass and are omitted from equilibrium expression; Reaction quotient Qc predicts shift direction: Qc < Kc shifts right (forward), Qc > Kc shifts left (reverse), Qc = Kc at equilibrium.
technical_core.why_required: Dynamic macroscopic invariance and mass-action equilibrium law.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Including concentrations of pure solids (e.g. CaCO3) or solvents in equilibrium constant expression.

mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Relation between Kp and Kc, and Reaction Quotient formula

symbols.name: Equilibrium Constant (Pressure)
symbols.dimension: Mass action constant in partial pressures

symbols.name: Gaseous Mole Change
symbols.dimension: Moles gaseous products - moles gaseous reactants

symbols.name: Reaction Quotient
symbols.dimension: Concentration ratio at any non-equilibrium instant

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Pure solids and liquids have activity = 1 and are excluded from Kc and Kp
mandatory_equations.conditions_of_validity: Reversible homogeneous or heterogeneous gas equilibrium

representations.name: Forward and Reverse Reaction Rates Equalizing at Dynamic Equilibrium
representations.chemistry_encoded: Rate vs time graph showing forward rate declining from maximum and reverse rate rising from zero until meeting at horizontal plateau (r_forward = r_reverse); alongside concentration vs time showing constant non-zero plateau
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Forward and reverse rates equalizing at non-zero value at equilibrium
representations.common_incorrect_version: Showing concentrations must be equal at equilibrium (confusing equal rates with equal concentrations)
representations.verification_method: Verify Kp = Kc (RT)^Delta n_g for N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3

model_conditions.condition: Equilibrium means forward rate EQUALS reverse rate; concentrations are CONSTANT, not necessarily equal.
model_conditions.why_needed: Pure solids (s) and pure liquids (l) have constant concentration and are omitted from Kc and Kp.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Kp = Kc (RT)^Delta n_g: if Delta n_g = 0, Kp = Kc unconditionally.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Write balanced equation and evaluate Delta n_g.
Write Kc expression omitting pure solids and liquids.
Calculate Qc and compare with Kc: Qc < Kc forward, Qc > Kc reverse.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Believing concentrations of reactants and products must be equal at equilibrium.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Confusing equality of rates with equality of concentrations.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal (rf = rr); concentrations can be vastly different (e.g. Kc = 10^10 means almost all product).
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: At equilibrium, rates are strictly equal, but concentrations are constant and determined by Kc.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-EQUIL-LAW-MASS-ACTION.

problem_families.name: Interconversion Between Kp and Kc and Direction Prediction
problem_families.recognition_cues: For N2(g) + 3 H2(g) <=> 2 NH3(g), calculate Kp given Kc = 0.5 at 400 K; predict shift if Qc = 2.0
problem_families.common_fatal_error: Using Delta n_g = +2 instead of -2

difficulty_profile.difficulty_basis: Dynamic mass action kinetics, pressure equilibria, and quotient directionality.

falsification_cases.authoring_defect: Including the molar concentration of solid CaCO3 in the equilibrium constant expression for CaCO3(s) <=> CaO(s) + CO2(g).
falsification_cases.expected_failure_reason: Pure solids have constant activity (unity) and must strictly be omitted from equilibrium constant expressions.

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Le Chatelier's Principle: Temperature, Pressure, Volume & Inert Gas Shifts

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: When a stress (concentration, pressure, volume, temperature) is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system shifts in the direction that counteracts the stress; Increasing pressure shifts toward fewer gaseous moles; Temperature changes the numerical value of K: for exothermic reactions (Delta H < 0), heating shifts left (decreases K); for endothermic (Delta H > 0), heating shifts right (increases K); Adding inert gas at constant volume has NO effect; adding inert gas at constant pressure increases total volume and shifts toward more gaseous moles; Catalysts accelerate both rates equally without shifting equilibrium position.
technical_core.why_required: Dynamic equilibrium perturbation and industrial yield optimization (Haber, Contact processes).
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Believing adding an inert gas at constant volume shifts the equilibrium position.

mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Van't Hoff Isobar Equation for Temperature Dependence of Equilibrium Constant

symbols.name: Equilibrium Constants
symbols.dimension: Values of K at temperatures T1 and T2

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Only temperature alters the numerical value of K; pressure, volume, catalyst do not change K
mandatory_equations.conditions_of_validity: Ideal gas equilibrium over moderate temperature range

representations.name: Concentration and Pressure Perturbation Response in Haber Synthesis
representations.chemistry_encoded: Response of N2(g) + 3 H2(g) <=> 2 NH3(g) (Delta H < 0) to: (1) increasing pressure (shifts right toward 2 moles), (2) increasing temperature (shifts left toward reactants, K decreases), (3) adding catalyst (reaches equilibrium faster, no shift)
mandatory_labels: N2 + 3 H2 <=> 2 NH3 + Heat (Delta H = -92 kJ/mol)
High Pressure Shift: Rightward (4 moles -> 2 moles)
High Temperature Shift: Leftward (Endothermic direction consumes added heat)
Catalyst Effect: Equal acceleration of kf and kr (K invariant)
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Clear illustration that catalyst does not shift equilibrium composition
representations.common_incorrect_version: Claiming a catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of ammonia
representations.verification_method: Verify Van't Hoff equation: heating exothermic reaction lowers K

model_conditions.condition: Only temperature changes the numerical value of the equilibrium constant K.
model_conditions.why_needed: Adding inert gas at constant volume does not change partial pressures of reacting gases; shift is ZERO.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Adding inert gas at constant pressure increases volume, lowering partial pressures; shifts toward MORE gas moles.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Examine perturbation: concentration, pressure/volume, inert gas, or temperature.
Check Delta n_g for pressure/volume shifts.
Check sign of Delta H for temperature shifts: heat acts as product for exothermic.
Recognize that catalysts never change equilibrium position or K.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Believing a catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of product in an industrial reaction.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Confusing reaction rate (kinetics) with equilibrium position (thermodynamics).
misconceptions.required_counterexample: A catalyst lowers activation energy equally for forward and reverse paths; it helps reach equilibrium faster but cannot alter the equilibrium constant K or yield.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: A catalyst speeds up the attainment of equilibrium without altering the equilibrium position or yield.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-EQUIL-LE-CHATELIER.

problem_families.name: Predicting Equilibrium Shift under Multiple Stresses
problem_families.recognition_cues: For N2(g) + 3 H2(g) <=> 2 NH3(g) (exothermic), predict effect of: (a) adding Ar at constant V, (b) increasing P, (c) heating
problem_families.first_technical_move: (a) Ar at constant V: no effect; (b) increasing P: shifts right (4 to 2 moles); (c) heating: shifts left (exothermic)
problem_families.common_fatal_error: Predicting shift upon adding inert gas at constant volume
problem_families.typical_unknown: Qualitative shift directions and K variation

difficulty_profile.difficulty_basis: Dynamic equilibrium perturbations, Van't Hoff temperature dependence, and industrial optimization.

falsification_cases.authoring_defect: Asserting that adding an inert gas (e.g. Helium or Argon) at constant volume shifts the equilibrium position.
falsification_cases.expected_failure_reason: Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not alter the partial pressures of the reactant and product gases, causing zero shift.

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Ionic Equilibrium: Ostwald Dilution Law, Ka/Kb & Weak Electrolyte pH

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: Weak electrolytes dissociate partially (alpha << 1); Ostwald's Dilution Law states degree of dissociation alpha = sqrt(Ka / C); as concentration C approaches 0 (infinite dilution), alpha approaches 1; For weak monobasic acid, [H+] = C alpha = sqrt(Ka * C) and pH = (1/2)(pKa - log10 C); Ka * Kb = Kw for conjugate acid-base pairs (pKa + pKb = 14 at 25 C).
technical_core.why_required: Equilibrium ionization of weak organic and inorganic electrolytes.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Applying strong acid complete dissociation [H+] = C to weak acids like acetic acid.

mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Ostwald Dilution Law and weak acid hydronium ion concentration
mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Approximation 1 - alpha approx 1 valid strictly when alpha <= 0.05 (5% rule); otherwise solve quadratic

representations.name: ICE (Initial, Change, Equilibrium) Table for Weak Monoprotic Acid Ionization
representations.chemistry_encoded: ICE table for HA(aq) <=> H+(aq) + A-(aq): Initial (C, 0, 0), Change (-C alpha, +C alpha, +C alpha), Equilibrium (C(1-alpha), C alpha, C alpha) with quadratic solution
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Proper ICE concentration bookkeeping across all stages
representations.common_incorrect_version: Assuming x = C (100% dissociation for weak acid)
representations.verification_method: Verify Ka * Kb == 10^-14 for conjugate acid-base pair at 25 C

model_conditions.condition: Approximation 1 - alpha approx 1 is valid only if alpha <= 0.05 (5% dissociation rule).
model_conditions.why_needed: If alpha > 0.05 (or C is very dilute), the exact quadratic equation C alpha^2 + Ka alpha - Ka = 0 must be solved.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Conjugate acid-base strength relationship: stronger the acid, weaker its conjugate base (pKa + pKb = 14).

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Set up ICE table with initial concentration C and dissociation x.
Write Ka = x^2 / (C - x).
Check 5% rule: if x/C < 0.05, approximate x = sqrt(Ka * C); else solve quadratic.
Compute pH = -log10(x).

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Calculating pH of 0.1 M CH3COOH as pH = -log(0.1) = 1.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Treating weak acetic acid as a strong acid with 100% dissociation.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: Acetic acid has Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5; [H+] = sqrt(1.8x10^-5 * 0.1) = 1.34 x 10^-3 M, giving pH = 2.87, not 1.0.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: Weak acids ionize partially; [H+] must be evaluated using Ka via Ostwald dilution, not initial concentration C.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-EQUIL-IONIC-PH-OSTWALD.

problem_families.name: pH and Degree of Ionization of Weak Acid
problem_families.recognition_cues: Calculate pH and degree of dissociation of 0.05 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5)
problem_families.common_fatal_error: Using strong acid assumption [H+] = 0.05 M -> pH = 1.3
problem_families.typical_unknown: Degree of dissociation alpha and pH

difficulty_profile.difficulty_basis: Ionic equilibrium, Ostwald dilution mathematics, and quadratic boundary testing.

falsification_cases.authoring_defect: Asserting 0.1 M acetic acid completely dissociates giving [H+] = 0.1 M and pH = 1.
falsification_cases.expected_failure_reason: Weak acids ionize partially according to Ostwald's dilution law; 0.1 M acetic acid yields pH approximately 2.87.

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Common Ion Effect, Buffer Solutions & Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: Common Ion Effect: addition of a salt containing a common ion suppresses dissociation of weak electrolyte (Le Chatelier shift); Buffer Solution resists pH change upon addition of small amounts of strong acid or base; Acidic buffer consists of weak acid + its conjugate salt (CH3COOH + CH3COONa); Basic buffer consists of weak base + conjugate salt (NH4OH + NH4Cl); Henderson-Hasselbalch equations: pH = pKa + log10([Salt]/[Acid]); Buffer capacity is maximized when [Salt] = [Acid] (pH = pKa).
technical_core.why_required: Acid-base buffering mechanisms in chemical and physiological systems (blood buffer).
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Calculating buffer pH by assuming added strong acid changes pH directly without buffer neutralization.

mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Henderson-Hasselbalch Buffer Equations

symbols.name: Conjugate Salt Molarity
symbols.dimension: Concentration of deprotonated conjugate base A-

symbols.name: Weak Acid Molarity
symbols.dimension: Concentration of protonated weak acid HA

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Valid within buffer capacity range pH = pKa +- 1

representations.name: Buffer Action Neutralization Mechanism and Titration Buffer Region
representations.chemistry_encoded: Diagram showing how buffer resists pH change: added H+ is absorbed by conjugate base A- (A- + H+ -> HA) and added OH- is neutralized by weak acid HA (HA + OH- -> A- + H2O), alongside titration curve showing flat buffer plateau around pH = pKa
mandatory_labels: Weak Acid Reserve: HA Neutralizes Added OH-
Conjugate Base Reserve: A- Neutralizes Added H+
Titration Buffer Plateau: Flat Region where pH = pKa +- 1
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Clear showing of both dual reserves (acid component and base component)
representations.common_incorrect_version: Drawing buffer curve without plateau or with steep vertical jump in buffer zone
representations.verification_method: Verify pH = pKa when [Salt] == [Acid]

model_conditions.condition: Buffer capacity is effective strictly within the range pH = pKa +- 1 (i.e. [Salt]/[Acid] ratio between 0.1 and 10).
model_conditions.why_needed: Maximum buffer capacity occurs when [Salt] = [Acid], where pH = pKa.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Common ion addition always suppresses ionization and decreases solubility of weak electrolytes.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Identify weak acid and conjugate salt concentrations.
Apply Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]).
For added strong acid/base, adjust moles of Acid and Salt stoichiometrically before recomputing pH.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Believing a mixture of strong acid and its salt (e.g. HCl + NaCl) functions as an acidic buffer.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Overlooking the requirement for a dynamic reversible equilibrium between weak acid and conjugate base.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: HCl is 100% dissociated; Cl- has zero basicity in water and cannot neutralize added H+; adding acid directly drops pH.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: Buffers strictly require a weak acid/base and its conjugate salt to maintain dual equilibrium reserves.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-EQUIL-BUFFERS-COMMON-ION.

problem_families.name: pH of Buffer and Effect of Strong Acid Addition
problem_families.recognition_cues: Calculate pH of buffer containing 0.1 M CH3COOH and 0.1 M CH3COONa (pKa = 4.74), and find pH after adding 0.01 mol HCl to 1 L
problem_families.common_fatal_error: Adding 0.01 M HCl directly to calculate pH = -log(0.01) = 2

difficulty_profile.difficulty_basis: Buffer thermodynamics, Henderson-Hasselbalch equilibrium, and common-ion suppression.

falsification_cases.authoring_defect: Classifying a solution of hydrochloric acid and sodium chloride (HCl + NaCl) as a buffer.
falsification_cases.expected_failure_reason: Buffers require a weak electrolyte and its conjugate species; strong acids cannot form buffer systems.

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Solubility Product (Ksp), Common Ion Suppression & Precipitation Criteria

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: For sparingly soluble salt AxBy(s) <=> x A^y+ + y B^x-, Solubility Product Ksp = [A^y+]^x [B^x-]^y = (x^x y^y) S^(x+y) where S is molar solubility; Ionic Product Qsp determines state: Qsp < Ksp (unsaturated, no precipitate), Qsp = Ksp (saturated equilibrium), Qsp > Ksp (supersaturated, precipitation occurs); Common ion effect severely suppresses solubility S.
technical_core.why_required: Precipitation equilibria, selective gravimetric precipitation, and qualitative inorganic analysis.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Comparing solubilities of salts of different stoichiometry directly by their Ksp values without computing S.

mandatory_equations.formula: K_{\text{sp}} = x^x y^y S^{x+y}, \quad Q_{\text{sp}} > K_{\text{sp}} \implies \text{Precipitation}
mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Solubility Product formula and Precipitation Criterion

symbols.name: Molar Solubility
symbols.dimension: Moles of salt dissolved per liter of saturated solution

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Pure solid salt AxBy(s) must be present at equilibrium; Ksp depends strictly on temperature

representations.name: Dynamic Saturated Salt Dissolution-Precipitation Equilibrium
representations.chemistry_encoded: Solid AgCl crystal at bottom of beaker in dynamic equilibrium with solvated Ag+(aq) and Cl-(aq) ions in solution, showing precipitation boundary when Qsp exceeds Ksp
mandatory_labels: Common Ion Effect: Adding NaCl drives Ag+ precipitation
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Dynamic balance of dissolving rate and recrystallization rate at saturation
representations.common_incorrect_version: Writing Ksp as a sum instead of a product of ion concentrations
representations.verification_method: Verify Ksp = 4 S^3 for 1:2 salt (like Mg(OH)2 or Ag2CrO4)

model_conditions.condition: Ksp expression involves powers equal to stoichiometric coefficients: for Ag2CrO4, Ksp = [Ag+]^2 [CrO4 2-] = (2S)^2 (S) = 4 S^3.
model_conditions.why_needed: Direct comparison of Ksp values to rank solubility is valid ONLY for salts of identical stoichiometry (e.g. AgCl vs AgBr).
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Precipitation occurs if and only if the ionic product Qsp strictly exceeds Ksp.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Write dissolution equation AxBy(s) <=> x A^y+ + y B^x-.
Express ion concentrations in terms of solubility S: [A] = xS, [B] = yS.
Calculate Ksp = (xS)^x (yS)^y = x^x y^y S^(x+y).
For common ion, substitute given ion concentration and solve for reduced S.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Claiming Ag2CrO4 (Ksp = 1.1 x 10^-12) is less soluble than AgCl (Ksp = 1.8 x 10^-10) because its Ksp is smaller.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Comparing Ksp values directly for salts of different stoichiometric types.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: For AgCl (1:1), S = sqrt(1.8e-10) = 1.34 x 10^-5 M; for Ag2CrO4 (2:1), S = (Ksp/4)^(1/3) = 6.5 x 10^-5 M; Ag2CrO4 is actually MORE soluble than AgCl.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: Salts of different stoichiometric types must be compared by computing their actual molar solubilities S, not by Ksp values directly.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-EQUIL-SOLUBILITY-PRODUCT.

problem_families.name: Molar Solubility in Pure Water vs Common Ion Solution

technical_core.canonical_statement: Balancing redox via Ion-Electron Method: divide into oxidation and reduction half-reactions; balance atoms other than H and O; balance O with H2O; balance H with H+ (in acid) or convert to OH- (in basic media); equalize electrons and sum; Galvanic Cell (Daniell cell: Zn | Zn2+ || Cu2+ | Cu) converts spontaneous chemical redox energy into electrical work; Anode is site of oxidation (negative electrode); Cathode is site of reduction (positive electrode); Salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality by ion migration and prevents liquid junction potential.
technical_core.why_required: Systematic electron conservation in redox balancing and electrochemical energy conversion.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Balancing half-reactions by adjusting subscripts instead of adding H2O / H+ / e-.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Separate overall reaction into oxidation and reduction half-reactions.
Balance half-reactions: elements -> O with H2O -> H with H+ -> charge with electrons.

misconceptions.required_counterexample: Electrons flow strictly through the external wire; in the salt bridge, current is carried entirely by the migration of mobile ions (K+ and Cl-).

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: IUPAC priority order determines principal functional group: -COOH > -SO3H > ester > acid chloride > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > C=C > C#C; Principal group takes suffix, all other groups become prefix substituents; Lowest locant rule applied to principal group first; Structural isomerism: Chain, Position, Functional group, Metamerism, Tautomerism; Geometrical isomerism (cis/trans, E/Z) requires restricted rotation (C=C) and two different groups on each double-bonded carbon.
technical_core.why_required: Systematic nomenclature of complex polyfunctional molecules and structural/spatial isomerism classification.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Assigning principal functional group suffix based on alphabetical order instead of IUPAC priority.

symbols.name: Double Bond Equivalent
symbols.dimension: Total count of rings plus pi bonds

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: DBE = 1 implies 1 double bond or 1 ring; DBE = 4 indicates benzene ring

trans-But-2-ene: Similar Groups on Opposite Sides (mu = 0, High MP)

representations.common_incorrect_version: Drawing cis/trans isomers for a compound with two identical groups on one carbon (e.g. propene)

model_conditions.condition: Geometrical isomerism requires restricted rotation AND each double-bonded carbon must have two DIFFERENT attached groups.
model_conditions.why_needed: If either carbon has two identical groups (e.g. (CH3)2C=CH2), geometrical isomerism CANNOT exist.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Tautomerism involves dynamic equilibrium between structural isomers differing in proton location (keto-enol).

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Calculate DBE = C + 1 - H/2 - X/2 + N/2 to identify rings/pi bonds.
Identify principal functional group by IUPAC priority hierarchy.
Number longest chain to give lowest locant to principal group.
Check geometrical isomerism requirement: abC=Ccd where a != b and c != d.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Claiming propene (CH3-CH=CH2) exhibits cis-trans geometrical isomerism.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Overlooking the requirement that BOTH carbons of the double bond must have two different groups.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: Terminal carbon of propene has two identical hydrogen atoms (=CH2); swapping them yields the identical molecule.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: Geometrical isomerism strictly requires that both double-bonded carbons carry two distinct groups (abC=Ccd).

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-ORGANIC-NOMENCLATURE-ISOMER.

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Electronic Displacements: Inductive, Resonance, Electromeric & Hyperconjugation
subtopic_gates.chapter: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: Inductive Effect (I): permanent polarization through sigma bonds due to electronegativity (-I: -NO2, -CN, -COOH, -X; +I: alkyl groups), weakens rapidly with distance (negligible beyond 3 carbons); Resonance / Mesomeric Effect (M/R): permanent delocalization of pi electrons through conjugated systems (+M: -OH, -NH2, -OR donate electrons by lone pair resonance; -M: -NO2, -CHO, -COOH withdraw electrons); Electromeric Effect (E): temporary complete transfer of pi electrons triggered by attacking reagent; Hyperconjugation (Baker-Nathan / No-bond resonance): sigma C-H electron delocalization into adjacent empty or partially filled p/pi* orbital, proportional to count of alpha-hydrogens.
technical_core.why_required: Fundamental electronic mechanisms explaining organic acidity, basicity, and reaction regioselectivity.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Applying inductive effect through multiple bonds while ignoring dominant resonance effect.

mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Hyperconjugation structure count and acid-strengthening relation

symbols.name: Alpha Hydrogens
symbols.dimension: Count of C-H bonds attached to adjacent sp3 carbon

symbols.name: Acidity Constant
symbols.dimension: Stabilized by -I and -M dispersing negative charge

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Resonance effect strictly dominates over inductive effect (except for halogens where -I dominates +M)

representations.name: Resonance Delocalization in Phenol vs Hyperconjugation in Ethyl Carbocation
representations.chemistry_encoded: Curved arrow electron flow in phenol showing +M lone pair donation into benzene ring generating ortho/para negative formal charges; alongside no-bond resonance in ethyl carbocation CH3-CH2+ showing sigma C-H bond overlap into vacant 2p orbital
mandatory_labels: Phenol +M Resonance: Ortho and Para Electron Rich
Ethyl Cation: 3 alpha-H giving 4 Hyperconjugative Forms
Inductive Distance Fall-off: C1 > C2 >> C3
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Curved arrows indicating electron pair movement and correct formal charges on resonance contributors
representations.common_incorrect_version: Moving atomic nuclei instead of electrons in resonance structures
representations.verification_method: Verify number of alpha-hydrogens matches stability order: 3 > 2 > 1 > methyl

model_conditions.condition: Resonance (+M/-M) operates strictly in conjugated planar systems and does NOT diminish with distance along conjugated chain.
model_conditions.why_needed: Inductive effect (-I/+I) operates through sigma bonds and diminishes rapidly, becoming negligible past 3 bonds.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Resonance effect generally dominates over inductive effect; notable exception: halogens on benzene where -I > +M.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Identify presence of conjugated pi systems (resonance) vs saturated sigma chains (inductive).
Count alpha-hydrogens on sp3 carbons adjacent to carbocation, radical, or alkene (hyperconjugation).
Compare relative acidities: electron-withdrawing groups (-I, -M) stabilize conjugate base and increase acidity.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Predicting that -OH on a benzene ring is deactivating because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Relying on inductive -I while overlooking powerful +M lone pair resonance donation.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: Oxygen donates its lone pair into the pi system via +M resonance, heavily activating the ring toward electrophilic attack despite -I.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: In aromatic systems, resonance (+M/-M) strongly dominates over inductive effects (except for halogens).

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-ORGANIC-ELECTRONIC-EFFECTS.

problem_families.common_fatal_error: Ranking trichloroacetic acid weaker than acetic acid
problem_families.typical_unknown: Acidity ranking and electronic effect justifications

difficulty_profile.difficulty_basis: Electron displacement dynamics, no-bond resonance, and charge dispersal.

falsification_cases.authoring_defect: Drawing resonance structures where atomic nuclei change positions.
falsification_cases.expected_failure_reason: Resonance structures differ strictly in the distribution of electrons; atomic nuclei must remain in fixed positions.

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Reaction Intermediates: Carbocations, Carbanions & Free Radicals Stability
subtopic_gates.chapter: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: Carbocation (R3C+): carbon has 6 valence electrons, sp2 hybridized, planar with empty p orbital; stability order: 3 > 2 > 1 > methyl (governed by hyperconjugation and +I); resonance-stabilized allylic and benzylic cations are exceptionally stable; undergo rearrangement (1,2-hydride and 1,2-methyl shifts) to form more stable carbocations; Free Radical (R3C*): 7 valence electrons, sp2 planar with single electron in p orbital, stability order: 3 > 2 > 1; Carbanion (R3C-): 8 valence electrons with 1 lone pair, sp3 pyramidal, stability order INVERTED: methyl > 1 > 2 > 3 (destabilized by +I alkyl electron donation).
technical_core.why_required: Reaction coordinate intermediate energetics, hybridization, and rearrangement pathways.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Applying carbocation stability order (3 > 2 > 1) to carbanions.

mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Comparative Stability Hierarchies of Reactive Organic Intermediates

symbols.name: Carbon Anion R3C-
symbols.dimension: Destabilized by +I alkyl groups; stabilized by -I/-M

symbols.name: Resonance Stabilized
symbols.dimension: More stable than simple alkyl intermediates

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Gas phase or solution phase with non-nucleophilic solvent

representations.name: 3D Hybridization and Orbital Geometries of Reactive Intermediates
representations.chemistry_encoded: Side-by-side geometries: Planar sp2 Carbocation with empty unhybridized p orbital; Planar sp2 Free Radical with half-filled p orbital containing 1 unpaired electron; Trigonal Pyramidal sp3 Carbanion with lone pair occupying hybrid orbital
mandatory_labels: Carbocation (sp2, 120): Empty p orbital perpendicular to plane
Free Radical (sp2, 120): Half-filled p orbital (1 e-)
Carbanion (sp3, ~107): Pyramidal geometry with lone pair
1,2-Hydride Shift: Migration of H- to form more stable 3 carbocation
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Accurate depiction of empty p orbital in carbocation and lone pair in pyramidal carbanion
representations.common_incorrect_version: Drawing carbocation as tetrahedral sp3 with 8 electrons
representations.verification_method: Verify alpha-H count for (CH3)3C+ = 9, (CH3)2CH+ = 6, CH3CH2+ = 3

model_conditions.condition: Carbocations undergo spontaneous 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shifts if rearrangement yields a more stable carbocation (e.g. 1 -> 3 or 2 -> 3).
model_conditions.why_needed: Carbanion stability is exactly inverted relative to carbocations because alkyl groups are electron-donating (+I), intensifying negative charge.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Allylic and benzylic carbocations are stabilized by resonance delocalization of positive charge across pi systems.

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Identify intermediate type: carbocation (+), carbanion (-), or radical (*).
Count alpha-hydrogens to rank carbocation or radical stability.
For carbocations, check for possible 1,2-hydride or 1,2-alkyl rearrangement to more stable intermediate.
For carbanions, invert alkyl stability order: methyl > 1 > 2 > 3.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Claiming tertiary carbanions are more stable than primary carbanions like carbocations.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Blindly applying carbocation rules to carbanions without considering charge polarity.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: In carbanions, carbon already carries an excess negative formal charge; electron-donating alkyl groups (+I) pump more electron density, destabilizing it.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: Carbanion stability order is strictly inverted (methyl > 1 > 2 > 3) because electron-donating alkyl groups destabilize negative charge.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-ORGANIC-INTERMEDIATES-STABILITY.

subtopic_gates.learner_title: Alkenes: Electrophilic Addition (Markovnikov vs Peroxide Effect) & Ozonolysis

provenance.source_curriculum: NCERT Grade 9-11 Chemistry / CBSE Secondary Curriculum

technical_core.canonical_statement: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition initiated by electrophile attacking pi bond; Markovnikov's Rule: in addition of unsymmetrical reagent (HX) to unsymmetrical alkene, acidic hydrogen/electrophile attaches to carbon with more hydrogens, generating more stable carbocation intermediate; Anti-Markovnikov (Kharasch Peroxide Effect) occurs strictly with HBr in presence of peroxides via free radical mechanism (fails for HCl and HI due to unfavorable thermodynamics); Ozonolysis (O3 followed by Zn/H2O) cleaves C=C double bond into carbonyl compounds (aldehydes/ketones), locating double bond position.
technical_core.why_required: Regioselective electrophilic additions and diagnostic oxidative cleavage of alkenes.
technical_core.failure_if_omitted: Applying peroxide effect (anti-Markovnikov) to HCl or HI.

mandatory_equations.formula: R-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{HX} \to R-\text{CHX}-\text{CH}_3, \quad R_1 R_2\text{C}=\text{CH} R_3 \xrightarrow[2. \, \text{Zn}/\text{H}_2\text{O}]{1. \, \text{O}_3} R_1 R_2\text{C}=\text{O} + \text{O}=\text{CH} R_3
mandatory_equations.meaning_of_symbols: Markovnikov addition and Reductive Ozonolysis cleavage

symbols.name: Unsymmetrical Alkene
symbols.dimension: Substrate with unequal hydrogen distribution on double bond

symbols.name: Reductive Workup
symbols.dimension: Prevents oxidation of aldehydes to carboxylic acids

symbols.name: Aldehyde / Ketone
symbols.dimension: Fragments locating original double bond position

mandatory_equations.reference_frame_or_sign: Peroxide effect operates strictly with HBr, NEVER with HCl or HI

representations.name: Two-Step Electrophilic Addition Mechanism Showing Carbocation Intermediate
representations.chemistry_encoded: Electrophilic attack of H+ on propene generating secondary isopropyl cation (stable, 6 alpha-H) rather than primary propyl cation (unstable, 2 alpha-H), followed by rapid nucleophilic attack of Br- to give 2-bromopropane; alongside ozonide ring cleavage by Zn/H2O
mandatory_labels: Step 1 (Slow RDS): H+ attacks C=C forming 2 Carbocation (Markovnikov)
Disfavored Path: H+ attacking C2 forming 1 Carbocation (Higher Ea)
Ozonolysis Cleavage: Slicing C=C bond to insert =O on each carbon
representations.what_cannot_be_omitted: Clear depiction of curved arrows and secondary carbocation intermediate
representations.common_incorrect_version: Showing anti-Markovnikov product as major product in absence of peroxides
representations.verification_method: Verify ozonolysis fragments reconstruct original alkene structure

model_conditions.condition: Peroxide effect (anti-Markovnikov) operates ONLY with HBr; HCl (H-Cl bond too strong, step 1 endothermic) and HI (I* radicals dimerize to I2, step 2 endothermic) ALWAYS follow Markovnikov addition even with peroxides.
model_conditions.why_needed: Zinc dust (Zn/H2O) in ozonolysis prevents H2O2 from oxidizing aldehydes to carboxylic acids.
model_conditions.what_changes_if_violated: Markovnikov rule is a direct consequence of carbocation stability (3 > 2 > 1).

reasoning_sequence.expert_action: Identify alkene symmetry: locate carbons with different numbers of hydrogens.
For HX without peroxide: apply Markovnikov (H goes to carbon with more H).
For HBr WITH peroxide: apply anti-Markovnikov free radical addition (Br goes to carbon with more H).
For ozonolysis: replace C=C double bond with two C=O carbonyl groups.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Applying the peroxide anti-Markovnikov effect to addition of HCl or HI.
misconceptions.why_plausible: Assuming the peroxide effect is a universal property of all hydrogen halides.
misconceptions.required_counterexample: H-Cl bond is too strong (431 kJ/mol) for propagation by alkoxy radicals; for HI, H-I addition is slow and iodine radicals dimerize into I2; only HBr has both propagation steps exothermic.
misconceptions.required_technical_repair: The peroxide effect (anti-Markovnikov addition) operates EXCLUSIVELY with HBr; HCl and HI always follow Markovnikov rule.

mandatory_verifications: Verify stoichiometry, mass conservation, and charge balance for CHEM-HYDROCARBONS-ALKENE-ADDITION.
